explanations.answer: A son's choices affect his parents
explanations.explanation: That's the one, friend. Solomon, David's son and Israel's king, says a wise son brings joy to his father, but a foolish son grief to his mother. Either way, the son's choices land on the people who love him. Nobody's choices stay in their own little corner.

explanations.answer: A son's choices only affect himself
explanations.explanation: Not quite, friend. Solomon, David's son and Israel's king, says a wise son brings joy to his father, and a foolish son brings grief to his mother. Joy and grief both land on somebody else. If a son's choices only touched himself, nobody's face would light up or fall.

explanations.answer: Parents decide how a son turns out
explanations.explanation: That one adds more than the verse says. Solomon, David's son and Israel's king, only tells us what a wise son brings his parents, joy, and what a foolish son brings, grief. The proverb never says who decides how he turns out. I'll stick with what's on the page, friend, and the page says a son's choices reach his parents.

Righteousness is the answer, baker! The verse says it flat out: "…righteousness brings deliverance from death." Treasure gotten the wrong way profits nothing, but righteousness actually delivers. One of those you can't take to the bank, and the other you don't have to.

Generosity sounds good, friend, and it's a nice word, but it's not the one Solomon picks. He says, "…righteousness brings deliverance from death." Righteousness is the word sitting right there in the second half of the line. Hold onto that one.
I love a good plan, friend. I've planned many a batch on the back of a napkin. But Solomon doesn't hang deliverance from death on planning. He says, "…righteousness brings deliverance from death."

Let me read you what Solomon really says, friend: "The LORD does not let the righteous go hungry, but He denies the craving of the wicked." That's the opposite of what the card said. The LORD is the one who doesn't let the righteous go hungry. Easy to flip when you're skimming, and I've flipped plenty of recipes the same way.

That's right, friend. Solomon says, "The LORD does not let the righteous go hungry, but He denies the craving of the wicked." So the righteous are not left hungry, and the craving of the wicked is the thing He denies. Two sides of one line, and you caught the right one.

explanations.answer: Work while the work is ready
explanations.explanation: You've got it, friend. The son who gathers in summer is wise, and the son who sleeps during harvest is disgraceful. The harvest is ready now, so that's when the gathering gets done. A harvest doesn't wait around for anybody to wake up.

explanations.answer: Rest whenever you feel worn out
explanations.explanation: I'd love that one, friend, I really would. But this proverb isn't about being worn out. It's about sleeping during harvest, and Solomon calls the son who does that a disgraceful son. The wise son is the one gathering when it's time to gather.

explanations.answer: Leave the harvest to hired hands
explanations.explanation: The verse doesn't mention hired hands at all, friend. It just sets two sons side by side: the one who gathers in summer is wise, and the one who sleeps during harvest is disgraceful. The picture is about being there when the harvest comes. So the lesson is to work while the work is ready.

True, baker! "The memory of the righteous is a blessing, but the name of the wicked will rot." Both halves are about what's left behind: the memory and the name. One is remembered as a blessing, and the other rots. I'd want to be the first kind of memory in any kitchen.

Look at the words again, friend. Solomon says, "The memory of the righteous is a blessing, but the name of the wicked will rot." Memory and name are both about how a person is remembered. So the proverb really is about what people remember of you.

That's flipped, friend. Solomon says, "He who walks in integrity walks securely, but he who perverts his ways will be found out." So the one who perverts his ways will be found out, not hidden forever. Integrity walks securely, and the other path catches up.

Right, friend, it's false. Solomon says, "…but he who perverts his ways will be found out." The one who bends his ways doesn't stay hidden. Meanwhile the one who walks in integrity walks securely, with nothing to dodge.

Covers is the word, baker! "Hatred stirs up dissension, but love covers all transgressions." Hatred stirs the pot, and love goes the other way. Notice it says all transgressions, so love's covering is not small.
Close in sound, friend, but the verse goes the other direction. Solomon says, "…but love covers all transgressions." Hatred is the one stirring up dissension. Love works the opposite way and covers.

Counting is what you'd expect from a stamper who tallies cookie boxes, friend, but Solomon doesn't use that word. He says, "…but love covers all transgressions." Love covers, and it covers all of them. Nobody's keeping a scoreboard in that line.

You spotted it, friend! The mouth and the lips keep showing up in these proverbs: the mouth of the wicked, foolish lips, the mouth of the righteous, the mouth of the fool. Mouths and lips are for speaking, so Solomon keeps his eye on what people say. Good thing that's the one part of me my mustache has to cover.

Mouths do eat, friend, and I'll admit mine's been in the chocolate chips. But in these proverbs the mouth and lips are tied to words. Solomon talks about the mouth that is a fountain of life, and foolish lips that come to ruin. That's about what people say.

Owning stuff isn't where these verses are looking, friend. Mouths and lips don't hold property. Solomon points at them again and again because of speech: the mouth of the righteous, foolish lips, the mouth of the fool. He's watching what people say.

His fortified city, that's right! Solomon says, "The wealth of the rich man is his fortified city, but poverty is the ruin of the poor." A fortified city has walls, so wealth works like walls for the rich man. The proverb is honest about how poverty hits the poor, too.

That's a fair guess, friend, but it's not Solomon's picture. He says, "The wealth of the rich man is his fortified city…" A city with walls is a place of protection. So he's talking about strength, not weight.
An open door is the opposite of what Solomon says, friend. He calls the rich man's wealth "his fortified city." Walls and gates, the kind built to keep things out. The picture is protection.

explanations.answer: Where each one's earnings take them
explanations.explanation: That's right, friend. The labor of the righteous leads to life, and the gain of the wicked brings punishment. Both of them earn something, and Solomon follows each paycheck to where it ends up. Same kind of work, very different destination.

The proverb doesn't name a boss, friend. It says the labor of the righteous leads to life, and the gain of the wicked brings punishment. Solomon is following what each one earns and where it leads. That's the comparison.

Shopping lists don't show up in this verse, friend. Solomon says, "The labor of the righteous leads to life, but the gain of the wicked brings punishment." The comparison is where the labor and the gain lead, which is life on one side and punishment on the other. Nobody's checking receipts.

Let's reread it together, friend. Solomon says, "Whoever heeds instruction is on the path to life, but he who ignores reproof goes astray." The one who ignores reproof doesn't stay on the path, he goes astray. Heeding instruction is the way that stays on.

Right, friend. Solomon says, "Whoever heeds instruction is on the path to life, but he who ignores reproof goes astray." So the one who ignores reproof goes astray, off the path. Heeding instruction is how a person stays on the path to life.

Restrained, baker, that's the word! Solomon says, "…he who restrains his lips is wise." When words are many, sin is unavoidable, so holding the lips back is the wise move. Sometimes the smartest thing in the room is a closed mouth.

Busy lips are the problem, friend, not the plan. Solomon says, "When words are many, sin is unavoidable, but he who restrains his lips is wise." The wise one holds his lips back. A lot of words doesn't make a lot of wisdom.

Wide open lips are what Solomon warns about, friend. He says, "When words are many, sin is unavoidable…" So the wise person does the opposite, as the verse finishes: "…he who restrains his lips is wise." Restrained is the word.

That's it, friend! Choice silver is silver of high quality, so the tongue of the righteous is valuable. Solomon says, "The tongue of the righteous is choice silver, but the heart of the wicked has little worth." One side is worth a lot, and the other has little worth. Easy to see which one I'd want in my bakery.

Cutting is not the picture here, friend. Solomon says, "The tongue of the righteous is choice silver, but the heart of the wicked has little worth." The next half of the line is about worth, and that's what silver is pointing at. Their words are valuable.

I get why shine came to mind, friend, silver does shine. But Solomon is comparing worth: "The tongue of the righteous is choice silver, but the heart of the wicked has little worth." There's nothing in the line about putting on a show. Their words are worth a lot.

Judgment is right, baker. Solomon says, "The lips of the righteous feed many, but fools die for lack of judgment." The righteous feed many with their words, and fools run out of the very thing they needed. It's a hard line, but it's a clear one.

Food is a clever guess, friend, since the first half says the lips of the righteous feed many. But the second half says fools "die for lack of judgment." The lack is judgment, not a pantry. Solomon is still talking about what people's lips and minds are doing.
Friends are nice to have, friend, but they aren't what this verse says fools lack. Solomon says, "…but fools die for lack of judgment." The missing thing is judgment. That's the word to hold onto.

That last part isn't what Solomon says, friend. He says, "The blessing of the LORD enriches, and He adds no sorrow to it." So the blessing comes with no sorrow added. Good thing I double-checked before I stamped it on a cookie.
Right, friend. Solomon says, "The blessing of the LORD enriches, and He adds no sorrow to it." The blessing enriches, and the LORD adds no sorrow to it. So sorrow doesn't come along with it.

That's it, baker. Solomon says, "What the wicked man dreads will overtake him, but the desire of the righteous will be granted." What he dreads catches up with him. On the other side, the righteous get what they desire.
Solomon says the opposite, friend. The verse reads, "What the wicked man dreads will overtake him…" The thing he dreads doesn't stay away. It catches up with him.

The verse doesn't say forgotten, friend. Solomon says, "What the wicked man dreads will overtake him…" Overtake is a running word, like something chasing him down and getting there. So what he dreads reaches him.

Hold on, friend, that's not what the verse says. Solomon says, "When the whirlwind passes, the wicked are no more, but the righteous are secure forever." The wicked are no more, and the righteous are secure. They don't get swept away together.

Right, friend. Solomon says, "When the whirlwind passes, the wicked are no more, but the righteous are secure forever." The whirlwind passes, the wicked are no more, and the righteous are still standing. Secure forever is a good place to be.

The slacker, you got it! Solomon says, "Like vinegar to the teeth and smoke to the eyes, so is the slacker to those who send him." Vinegar on your teeth, smoke in your eyes, that's how the one who sent him feels. Both are irritating, and neither goes away quickly.

Mockers show up elsewhere in Proverbs, friend, but not in this verse. Solomon says, "Like vinegar to the teeth and smoke to the eyes, so is the slacker to those who send him." The one sent on the job and not getting it done is the slacker.

Gossip is a good guess in a chapter full of lips, friend, but this verse has someone else in mind. Solomon says, "…so is the slacker to those who send him." The slacker is the one who gets sent and lets it slide. Vinegar and smoke are what he is to the ones who sent him.

Nothing, baker, that's the idea! Solomon says, "The hope of the righteous is joy, but the expectations of the wicked will perish." What the wicked are counting on perishes. The righteous end up with joy.

Come to pass sounds like a real saying, friend, and it's a good one. But it means a thing happens, and Solomon says the opposite. He says, "…the expectations of the wicked will perish." So the word that fits is nothing.

Come to light is a real saying too, friend, but it's not what this verse means. Solomon says, "The hope of the righteous is joy, but the expectations of the wicked will perish." Their expectations perish, which is the same as coming to nothing.

Destruction, that's right, baker. Solomon says, "The way of the LORD is a refuge to the upright, but destruction awaits those who do evil." The same way of the LORD that shelters the upright sits across from destruction. A refuge on one side, and on the other, something waiting.
That sounds generous, friend, but it's not in this verse. Solomon says, "…but destruction awaits those who do evil." Destruction is the word on the other side from refuge.
A quiet life sounds nice, friend, I'd take one myself. But Solomon doesn't say that about those who do evil. He says, "…but destruction awaits those who do evil." Refuge is for the upright.

True, baker. Solomon says, "The mouth of the righteous brings forth wisdom, but a perverse tongue will be cut out." The mouth brings forth wisdom, and a perverse tongue is cut out. Words in these proverbs carry real consequences, and Solomon says it more than once in this chapter.

Take another look, friend. Solomon says, "The mouth of the righteous brings forth wisdom, but a perverse tongue will be cut out." One mouth brings forth wisdom, and one tongue is cut out. If words had no consequences, that line wouldn't need to say either one.
